Al-Tabari retient la lecture des grandes villes. Quant à la fonction grammaticale de « qurbanan », al-Zamakhshari en fait un complément de manière et rejette qu'il soit un second complément, alors qu'Ibn ʿAtiyya et Abu Hayyan l'admettent sans que le sens soit altéré selon eux.

Ce verset rappelle que Dieu a anéanti les cités voisines de La Mecque, comme 'Ad, Thamud, Sodome ou Ma'rib, après leur avoir exposé des signes et des preuves afin qu'elles reviennent de leur mécréance. Il demande ensuite, sur le ton du reproche : pourquoi les divinités qu'ils avaient prises en dehors de Dieu, comme moyens de rapprochement, ne les ont-elles pas secourus ? La réponse implicite est qu'elles les ont abandonnés et ont disparu à leur heure, et que cela résulte de leur mensonge et de leurs inventions. Les commentateurs s'accordent à y voir une mise en garde adressée aux Qurayshites, et une moquerie des idoles incapables d'intervenir lors du châtiment. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir et Ibn al-Jawzi précisent que les cités désignées sont celles de 'Ad, Thamud, du peuple de Lot et de Madian, alors que Ibn Juzayy et Abu Hayyan estiment qu'il s'agit d'une comparaison avec Ma'rib, Hijr, Thamud et Sodome. Quant au mot 'qurbanan', al-Zamakhshari et al-Nasafi l'expliquent comme 'ce par quoi l'on se rapproche de Dieu', et y voient un complément de situation ; Ibn 'Atiyya et Abu Hayyan admettent qu'il puisse être le second complément du verbe, ce que rejette al-Zamakhshari pour incohérence du sens. Pour la lecture de 'ifkuhum', la majorité lit 'ifkuhum' avec kasra et sukun, tandis qu'Ibn 'Abbas et d'autres lisent 'afakahum' au sens de les détourner de la vérité ; al-Tabari retient la lecture des grands centres. Al-Razi et al-Alusi relèvent l'ironie du passage, l'impossibilité de tout secours, et les différentes interprétations de 'ma kanu yaftarun', qui peut être une proposition verbale ou relative.

Ce verset rappelle qu'un groupe de djinns, moins de dix, fut dirigé vers le Prophète ﷺ alors qu'il récitait le Coran. Lorsqu'ils furent présents, ils se dirent les uns aux autres : taisez-vous et écoutez. Quand la récitation fut achevée, ils retournèrent vers leur peuple en les avertissant. Les commentateurs s'accordent à dire que le passage vise à réprimander les Quraych qui ne crurent pas, alors que les djinns crurent. Ils divergent sur les circonstances. Ibn 'Abbas et Sa'id ibn Jubayr rapportent que les djinns, chassés par les météores qui gardaient désormais le ciel, cherchèrent la cause et trouvèrent le Prophète priant l'aube à Nakhla, sans qu'il les remarque. D'autres, dont Ibn Mas'ud, rapportent que le Prophète fut chargé de réciter aux djinns, que Ibn Mas'ud le suivit, qu'il tracé un cercle autour de lui, puis qu'il entendit un grand tumulte, et que le Prophète expliqua qu'il avait jugé un différend entre eux au sujet d'un tué. Sur leur nombre, Ibn 'Abbas dit sept de Nisibe, Zirr ibn Hubayš dit neuf dont Zawba'a, 'Ikrima dit douze mille. Sur leur récompense, Abu Hanifa soutient qu'ils n'ont d'autre récompense que d'être sauvés du feu, alors que Malik, al-Shafi'i et Ibn Abi Layla estiment qu'ils sont récompensés pour le bien comme ils sont punis pour le mal. Les djinns déclarent que le Livre confirme ce qui le précède et guide vers la vérité et le chemin droit, et ils exhortent leur peuple à répondre à l'appel de Dieu et à croire, car celui qui ne répond pas est dans un égarement évident.

Ce verset rapporte les paroles qu'un groupe de djinns adressa à leur peuple après avoir écouté la récitation du Prophète ﷺ. Ils disent avoir entendu un Livre révélé après Moïse, qui confirme les Écritures antérieures, guide vers la vérité et vers une voie droite. Les commentateurs s'accordent à y voir le Coran et à considérer que les djinns ont transmis à leur peuple un message d'avertissement. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir et al-Baghawi rapportent que ces djinns venaient de Nisibe, de Ninive ou de la région de Mossoul, et que leur nombre varie selon les transmissions : sept ou neuf selon Ibn Abbas, Mujahid et Zirr ibn Hubaysh, douze mille selon Ikrima. Beaucoup estiment que le Prophète ne les remarqua pas d'abord, tandis qu'al-Hasan al-Basri affirme qu'il n'apprit leur présence que par révélation. Quant à la mention de Moïse sans Jésus, Ibn Abbas l'explique par le fait que les djinns n'avaient pas entendu parler de Jésus ; al-Zamakhshari, al-Biqa'i et Ibn Kathir y voient plutôt la primauté de la Torah comme fondement de la loi. Sur la récompense des djinns croyants, Abu Hanifa soutient qu'ils n'obtiennent que le salut du feu, tandis que Malik, al-Shafi'i et Ibn Abi Layla les considèrent comme les humains, récompensés pour le bien et punis pour le mal ; Ibn Kathir s'appuie sur la sourate Ar-Rahman pour affirmer leur entrée au Paradis. Ibn Kathir et al-Bayhaqi rapportent que des délégations de djinns vinrent ensuite auprès du Prophète à plusieurs reprises, probablement avant l'Hégire.

Ce passage rapporte les paroles des djinns qui, après avoir écouté le Coran puis regagné leur peuple en avertisseurs, leur ont dit : répondez à l'appel de Dieu, c'est-à-dire du Prophète Muhammad ﷺ, en croyant et en obéissant à ce qu'il enseigne ; Dieu vous pardonnera une partie de vos péchés et vous préservera d'un châtiment douloureux. Les commentateurs s'accordent sur ce sens apparent : l'appel à la foi et à l'obéissance, avec la promesse du pardon et du salut du Feu. Plusieurs, tels qu'al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Nasafi, al-Shawkani, Ibn Juzayy et Abu Hayyan, relèvent que le mot « min » dans « de vos péchés » indique une partie, ce qui signifie, selon eux, que les torts envers les hommes ne sont pardonnés qu'après restitution à leurs ayants droit. Al-Zamakhshari et Ibn 'Atiyya expliquent aussi cette particule comme partitive, car la foi n'efface pas tout ; d'autres, comme al-Zamakhshari dans une de ses variantes et Ibn Hayyan, la jugent parfois superflue ou de début de domaine. Sur la récompense des djinns croyants, les avis divergent : Abu Hanifa, rapporté par al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir et al-Qurtubi, estime qu'ils n'obtiennent que le salut du Feu ; al-Malik, al-Shafi'i et Ibn Abi Layla affirment qu'ils sont récompensés comme les humains, tandis que al-Dahhak rapporte qu'ils entrent au Paradis. Ibn Kathir s'appuie sur le verset de la Sourate al-Rahman pour soutenir l'entrée des croyants parmi eux au Paradis. Quant à la phrase « Quiconque ne répond pas à l'appel de Dieu ne peut réduire Dieu à l'impuissance sur terre », elle avertit qu'on ne peut échapper à Dieu par la fuite, qu'on n'a aucun protecteur en dehors de Lui, et que ceux qui refusent sont dans un égarement manifeste. Plusieurs commentateurs rapportent que ces djinns venaient de Nisibe ou de Ninive, que l'épisode eut lieu à Batn Nakhla lors de la prière de l'aube, et diffèrent sur la présence d'Ibn Mas'ud, point qui n'affecte pas directement le sens du verset.

Le sens apparent du verset est que celui qui ne répond pas à l'appel de Dieu, transmis par son Prophète ﷺ, ne pourra échapper à Dieu sur terre, et n'aura personne en dehors de Lui pour le protéger ; ceux-là sont dans un égarement manifeste. Les commentateurs rattachent ce passage au récit des djinns qui ont écouté le Coran et sont repartis avertir leur peuple. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir et al-Baghawi expliquent que « ne pas répondre » signifie ne pas croire ni obéir, et que nul ne peut fuir la puissance divine. Ibn Jurayj et Ibn 'Ashur rapportent que le verset peut être une parole des djinns ou de Dieu lui-même ; Ibn Kathir et Ibn Jurayj n'en tirent pas de loi. Le débat le plus notable porte sur le sort des djinns croyants : Abu Hanifa soutient qu'ils ne reçoivent d'autre récompense que d'être sauvés du feu, alors qu'al-Razi, al-Qurtubi, Malik et Ibn Abi Layla estiment qu'ils sont soumis aux mêmes récompenses et châtiments que les hommes. Ibn Kathir, lui, penche pour l'entrée des croyants parmi les djinns au Paradis, sans trancher définitivement. Quant au sens de « min » dans « min dhunubikum », al-Zamakhshari et Ibn Juzayy y voient un partitif, excluant les torts envers autrui, tandis qu'al-Razi le considère comme un indicateur de début. Ces débats ne portent pas sur le sens général du verset, qui reste le même pour tous.

Dans ce verset, Dieu rappelle à ceux qui nient la résurrection qu'ils n'ont pas réfléchi au fait que Celui qui a créé les cieux et la terre, sans être fatigué ni épuisé par cette création, est capable de ressusciter les morts. Les commentateurs expliquent que le verbe « ya'ya » signifie être las ou être incapable, que la question est de réprobation, et que le « bala » final affirme la puissance de Dieu sur toute chose. Tous s'accordent à voir dans ce verset un argument pour la résurrection, qui procède du plus grand au moindre : celui qui peut créer les cieux et la terre peut recréer l'être humain. Les grammairiens débattent de la présence du « ba » dans « bi-qadir ». Abu 'Ubayda et al-Akhfash y voient une particule de renforcement. Al-Kisa'i, al-Farra' et al-Zajjaj l'expliquent par la négation qui précède « inna » : le sens serait « Dieu n'est-il pas capable ? ». Al-Tabari retient ce dernier avis comme le plus juste. Ibn Kathir rapporte que Dieu dit aux cieux et à la terre « Soyez », et qu'ils obéissent sans effort. Pour conclure, les exégètes soulignent que cette puissance s'étend à toute chose et que nier la résurrection revient à nier l'étendue de la puissance divine.

Le verset décrit la scène du Jour de la Résurrection où les mécréants sont présentés au Feu. On leur demande, pour les réprimander, si ce châtiment n'est pas la vérité ; ils confessent alors : « Oui, par notre Seigneur ! » et il leur est dit : « Goûtez donc le châtiment pour avoir mécru. » Les commentateurs s'accordent à y voir une réprimande et une raillerie à l'égard de ceux qui se moquaient de la promesse et de la menace divines, et une confession arrivée trop tard pour être utile. Al-Hasan al-Basri rapporte qu'ils subiront le châtiment en étant satisfaits, reconnaissant la justice de Dieu. Quant à l'ordre de patienter « comme ont patienté les messagers doués de résolution », les avis divergent sur leur identité : Ibn Zayd, al-Tabari et Ibn al-Anbari estiment qu'il s'agit de tous les messagers, la particule « min » étant alors explicative et non partitive ; Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada et Mujahid citent Noé, Abraham, Moïse, Jésus et Muhammad ; Muqatil en compte six, al-Hasan al-Basri quatre, et al-Hasan ibn al-Fadl les dix-huit prophètes de la sourate des Bestiaux. Tous s'accordent sur le sens de la patience face à l'offense et à l'effort, et sur l'interdiction de hâter le châtiment pour les opposants. Les mécréants, disent-ils, auront l'impression de n'être restés dans le monde qu'une heure du jour. Sur le mot « balagh », certains y voient le Coran ou la transmission du message, d'autres la durée de la vie terrestre. Le verset se clôt par une menace pour les pervers, et plusieurs y voient un motif d'espérance pour les croyants.

Ce verset ordonne au Prophète ﷺ de persévérer face à l'hostilité de son peuple, comme l'ont fait les messagers dotés de constance, et de ne pas hâter le châtiment destiné aux incroyants, qui viendra inévitablement. Les commentateurs expliquent que, le jour où ils verront ce châtiment, ces gens auront l'impression de n'être restés dans ce monde qu'une heure d'un jour. Le verset conclut que le Coran est un message transmis, et que seuls périssent les pervers qui sortent de l'obéissance à Dieu.

Les exégètes s'accordent sur le sens de la patience demandée : la persévérance dans la transmission du message et la résistance aux offenses. En revanche, l'identité des « messagers dotés de constance » fait l'objet de nombreux avis. Ibn Abbas, Qatada, Ata al-Khurasani et Ibn Kathir retiennent Noé, Abraham, Moïse, Jésus et Muhammad ﷺ. Al-Kalbi, Muqatil et al-Hasan ibn al-Fadl donnent des listes plus longues, parfois de dix-huit prophètes. Ibn Zayd et Ibn al-Anbari estiment que « min » est explicatif et non partitif, de sorte que tous les messagers seraient concernés.

Sur le mot « balagh », al-Tabari, Ibn al-Jawzi et Ibn Kathir proposent deux lectures : il désigne soit le Coran et son message, soit la courte durée de séjour évoquée juste avant. Le verset se termine par une formule que beaucoup, comme Qatada, lisent comme porteuse d'espoir : ne périt devant Dieu que celui qui le mérite.

The commentators explain that this opening verse of Surat al-Ahqaf affirms that the Book is a revelation from God, the Mighty, the Wise, and that the heavens, the earth and all that lies between them were not created in vain but with truth, for a fixed term. Most take this term to be the Day of Resurrection, following Ibn 'Abbas as reported by al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir, while others understand it as the appointed end of every creature. The verse then states that the disbelievers turn away from the warning they have received, namely the resurrection and the reckoning.

The commentators agree that the verse offers an argument for monotheism and for the resurrection: a universe created with truth reveals the wisdom of its Creator. Al-Razi draws from it proofs of God's existence, His justice and His mercy, and the duty to reflect and reason. Al-Zamakhshari notes that the word "ma" may be a verbal noun, meaning "of their warning".

The disagreements concern the following verse, which is linked to this one in context. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir judge that the most sound meaning of "athara" is a remnant of knowledge. Ibn 'Abbas and al-Baghawi understand it as the line drawn in the sand, Mujahid as knowledge transmitted from earlier people, Qatada as a special knowledge, and al-Hasan as knowledge one brings forth.

This summary does not decide between these views; it reports the meanings the text can bear, while the general sense of the opening verse is shared by all.

The verse states that the Book is a revelation sent down by God, the Mighty, the Wise: Mighty in His dominion, which cannot be overcome, and Wise in His making and governing. The commentators read it as a bridge to the next verse, which reminds the reader that God created the heavens, the earth and what lies between them only in truth and for a set term. Al-Tabari understands "truth" as justice and the establishment of right, while al-Mawardi gives several meanings: sincerity, justice, and the purpose of resurrection. Ibn Kathir and al-Tabari say creation is not idle play. As for the set term, Ibn Abbas and al-Baghawi identify it as the Day of Resurrection, which brings the world to its end, while al-Mawardi also reports the view that it is the term decreed for every creature. The verse ends by noting that the disbelievers turn away from the warning they were given. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Atiyya observe that "ma" may be read as a verbal particle or as a relative pronoun. The commentators do not settle between these readings and leave the reader to weigh them.

This verse states that God created the heavens, the earth and what lies between them only in truth, meaning not in vain or as play, but with wisdom and purpose. He appointed for this creation a term known to Him. Most commentators, including Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi, take this term to be the Day of Resurrection, while Ibn 'Abbas explains it as the end of the heavens and the earth, and others as the fixed lifespan of every creature. Al-Tabari understands 'truth' as the establishment of justice among creatures, while al-Razi derives from it proof of a wise, merciful and just Creator and of the Resurrection. Ibn 'Ashur and Ibn Sa'di likewise link the creation to the principle of recompense. The verse then says that the disbelievers turn away from what they were warned of. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and al-Nasafi explain that they neither reflect nor heed the warning and do not prepare for it. The commentators differ mainly on the particle 'ma'. Some read it as a relative pronoun meaning what they were warned about, others as a verbal noun meaning the act of warning, as al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu al-Su'ud note, considering both readings valid. The overall meaning remains the same: a universe created with wisdom and bounded by a term, facing people who turn away from this truth.

God instructs His Messenger to confront the polytheists with a question that exposes the baselessness of worshipping idols: what have the beings they invoke created from the earth, or do they have any share in creating the heavens? He then challenges them to bring a Book revealed before the Quran that commands such worship, or some remnant of knowledge that supports it. The commentators, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Nasafi, Ibn Juzayy and al-Alusi, agree that the verse is a challenge and a rebuke: the idols create nothing and have no share in creation, and all revealed scriptures forbid associating partners with God. Al-Mawardi and Ibn al-Jawzi list several meanings of the word athara. The majority reading means a remnant of knowledge, which al-Tabari prefers, citing Arabic usage and a line of al-Ra'i's poetry. Mujahid understands it as knowledge handed down by earlier generations, al-Hasan as something brought out and stirred up, and Qatada as a special portion of knowledge. Ibn Abbas, as transmitted by several scholars, takes it to mean the lines drawn in sand used in divination, and cites a hadith; al-Razi reads this as mockery. Ibn 'Ashur holds that it refers to an oral tradition never written down. The variant readings athara and athra carry closely related meanings, such as a particular knowledge given to some. All agree that whoever creates nothing does not deserve worship.

This verse states that no one is more astray than one who calls upon, besides God, deities that will never answer him, until the Day of Resurrection. Most commentators understand these to be idols. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that describing them as heedless of their worshippers' calls is a comparison with a distracted person who does not understand what is said to him, since these idols are stone or wood that neither hear nor understand. For them the verse is a rebuke to the polytheists for their poor judgement and their choice of worship. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi note that the Quran addresses the idols in the grammatical form used for rational beings, because the idolaters treated them as masters, like kings and princes who are served. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi hold that the wording may include every object of worship besides God, such as the angels, Jesus and Uzayr, with the idols singled out as the primary target. Al-Razi and Ibn 'Ashur take the phrase 'until the Day of Resurrection' to mean the whole duration of this world, and they add that on that Day the worshipped will disown their worshippers, a point also made by Ibn Kathir and al-Zamakhshari. Among modern writers, Sayyid Qutb widens the verse to cover any power or wealth invoked besides God, whereas al-Jaza'iri and the King Fahd Complex restrict it to the dead, stones and trees. The commentators do not draw any legal ruling from the verse.

This verse describes the Day of Resurrection, when people are gathered and those they worshipped besides God become their enemies and disown their worship. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that this refers to the idols, which will disclaim their worshippers because they never commanded the worship and were not aware of it. Al-Baghawi cites a parallel verse in which the worshippers say they disown what they used to worship, while Sayyid Qutb and Ibn Sa'di stress that these deities have no power whatsoever to benefit or harm.

The commentators broadly agree on the overall meaning: idolatry turns against its followers, and worshipping beings that cannot answer is a plain error. Al-Qurtubi and al-Nasafi note that the verse continues the earlier point that these deities never respond to prayer. Ibn Ashur observes that the language of enmity may be a forceful comparison rather than real hostility, since these idols become a source of ruin for those who serve them.

The main point of disagreement concerns who is meant by those worshipped. Al-Razi reports that most scholars hold that God will bring the idols back to life on that day, while others say the verse refers to angels and Jesus. Abu Hayyan and Ibn Juzayy explain that the idols are referred to with the words used for rational beings, since they are treated as such in the pagans' beliefs; Ibn Ashur adds that the term may cover anything worshipped besides God. As for the pronouns of "they were", Abu al-Su'ud and al-Alusi note that they could refer to the worshippers, who would then deny their idolatry, but al-Alusi and al-Qasimi find this reading weaker because it departs from the context.

This passage of Surat al-Ahqaf describes how the disbelievers react when Allah's clear verses are recited to them: they immediately call the Quran plain magic, without reflection. The commentators explain that "the truth" refers to the verses or the Quran, and that the preposition "li" expresses cause, meaning "on account of the truth" or "concerning it"; al-Shawkani and al-Sha'rawi take it as "about", while Ibn 'Ashur links it to those who believed. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir report that the unbelievers called the Quran sorcery, and al-Zamakhshari notes that their haste to reject it without thought reveals their stubbornness and wrongdoing. When they claim Muhammad invented it, al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir explain that God commands the Prophet to reply that, had he forged it, no one could shield him from divine punishment, that God knows what they say, and that He suffices as a witness between them. Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi observe that the verse warns and then invites repentance through the attributes of forgiveness and mercy. On "I am not a novelty among the messengers", Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada take it to mean that he is not the first messenger. Regarding "I do not know what will be done with me or with you", opinions differ: al-Hasan, Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada apply it to the Hereafter, a view later clarified by the verses of victory, while al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir relate it to worldly life, such as exile, killing or punishment, and others to commands and prohibitions. The verse concludes that the Prophet follows only what is revealed to him and is only a clear warner.

This verse reports the claim of the polytheists that the Prophet had invented the Qur'an himself. The commentators explain that God commanded him to answer with a hypothesis: if he had truly fabricated it, God would punish him, and no one could shield him from that punishment, so why would he expose himself to it? Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Nasafi take 'He knows best what you spread about it' to mean your talk disparaging the Qur'an, calling it sorcery at one time and fabrication at another. They also agree that God bears witness to the Prophet's truthfulness and to his delivery of the message, and that He bears witness against those who deny it. The closing words, 'He is the Forgiving, the Merciful', are read by most as an invitation to repentance and to abandon disbelief, along with a sign of God's forbearance despite the gravity of their sins. Opinions differ on what the pronoun in 'he has invented it' refers to: Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan take it to refer to the truth, meaning the verses, while others take it to refer to the Qur'an. Al-Zamakhshari suggests that attributing the act to the interlocutors serves to highlight, by contrast, the fate of the one who fabricates. Ibn 'Ashur sees in this passage a shift toward an even graver accusation, while Ibn Sa'di and al-Sha'rawi stress the courtesy of the dialogue, with the Prophet remaining measured before accusers who called him a liar.

God tells His Prophet to say to the idolaters of his people that he is not the first of the messengers, since many were sent before him, that he does not know what will be done to him or to them, that he follows only what is revealed to him, and that he is a clear warner. The commentators largely agree on the general sense. Al-Hasan al-Basri, al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir understand the verse as concerning worldly affairs: the Prophet does not know whether he will be expelled or killed, or what will befall the two sides in victory or punishment. Ibn Kathir considers this the only fitting reading, since the Prophet was certain of his destiny in the Hereafter. Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada, 'Ikrima and Anas, by contrast, take it to concern the Hereafter, and say it was abrogated by the verse that God has forgiven the Prophet his past and future sins. They cite the story of the death of 'Uthman ibn Maz'un. Al-Tabari and al-Qurtubi reject abrogation of a statement of fact, and some answer that the verse denies only detailed knowledge. Al-Kalbi gives a different occasion: the Prophet had seen in a dream a land of palm trees to which he would emigrate, and when this was delayed and he stayed silent before his companions' questions, the verse was revealed. Al-Dahhak reads it as saying he does not know what he and they will be commanded or forbidden. All agree that the Prophet follows only revelation and that his role is to warn.

God instructs His Prophet to confront the idolaters with a concrete argument: tell me, if the Quran is from God and you disbelieve in it, and a witness from the Children of Israel bears witness to its like, believes, while you grow arrogant, are you not in error and wrongdoing? The commentators agree that the answer to the conditional is omitted and is implied by the closing words, God does not guide the wrongdoers; some supply, are you not wrongdoers? others, who then is more astray than you? As for the witness, the majority, including Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, Mujahid, Qatada, Ibn Sirin, Ibn Zayd and Malik, identify him as Abdullah ibn Salam, who testified that Muhammad is mentioned in the Torah and embraced Islam. Masruq and al-Sha'bi object that the sura is Meccan while he converted in Medina, and hold that the witness is Moses, who attested to the Torah, which resembles the Quran in its doctrine of God's oneness, promise and warning. al-Tabari favours this reading, while others consider the verse Medinan inserted into a Meccan sura, or leave the witness unspecified. The disbelievers' claim that had it been good, they would not have been preceded to it, is taken by most as aimed at the poor and weak believers; Ibn Kathir sees in it the arrogance that rejects truth. Their saying it is an ancient lie means it resembles old tales. The verse adds that the Torah was a guide and mercy, and that the Arabic Quran confirms it, to warn the wrongdoers and give good news to the righteous.

The commentators explain that this verse reports the words of those who rejected faith, said to those who believed: if what Muhammad brought were good, we would have reached it before you, the people of standing and prestige. Because they were not guided by the Qur'an, they call it an ancient lie, like the fables of the ancients. The commentators disagree about who is meant. Qatada, al-Kalbi, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi understand the speakers as the leaders of Mecca, who were referring to Bilal, 'Ammar, Suhayb and similar weak believers; Ibn Juzayy considers this the strongest view because the surah is Meccan. Masruq and others take the speakers to be the Jews, and the believers to be 'Abd Allah ibn Salam and his companions. Al-Kalbi and others name Arab tribes who mocked Juhayna, Muzayna, Ghifar and Aslam when they embraced Islam. Several occasions of revelation are reported, such as the story of 'Umar's slave-woman or Zunayra, whose sight God restored, but most commentators do not draw a general rule from these reports.

The commentaries agree that the verse condemns the arrogance of these people and their attachment to worldly rank, and that their refusal of guidance is what leads them to dismiss the Qur'an as falsehood. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Alusi and Abu Hayyan take the verb governed by 'idh' to be implied, while Ibn Juzayy reads 'idh' as meaning 'because', and Ibn 'Ashur explains that the future form 'sayaqulun' shows that this speech will continue. Ibn Kathir links the attitude to the hadith that pride is rejecting the truth and despising people.

The verse then turns to the Book of Moses as a guide and mercy, and to the Qur'an, which confirms it in the Arabic tongue, to warn the wrongdoers and give good news to the doers of good. It ends with those who say 'Our Lord is God' and then remain upright: they will have no fear and no sorrow, which the commentators connect with faith and obedience.

The commentators explain that this verse reminds that the Book of Moses, the Torah, came before the Quran as a guide to be followed and a mercy for those who believed in it, and that the Quran came confirming it and the Scriptures before it, in clear Arabic. Most, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi, agree that the pronoun "before it" refers to the Quran, that "a guide and a mercy" are circumstantial terms, and that "in Arabic tongue" describes either the Book or the verb "confirming". The purpose of its revelation is to warn those who wronged themselves through polytheism and disobedience, and to give good news to the doers of good, meaning the believers who did well in their faith and deeds. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi note that the warning and the good news explain each other, since the wrongdoers are contrasted with the doers of good.

The disagreements concern grammar and recitation. Al-Tabari treats "in Arabic tongue" as a circumstantial term, whereas al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya allow it to be the object of "confirming", referring then to the Prophet ﷺ; Ibn al-Qayyim holds that the circumstantial term relates to the Book, since it is specified by its attribute. On the reading of "that he may warn", Nafi', Ibn Amir and others read it in the second person, addressing the Prophet, while most read it in the third person, referring to the Book; Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim prefer the second-person reading.

Other points, such as some elliptical constructions, are also discussed by the exegetes, who leave their precise intent to God.

This verse states that those who say "Our Lord is Allah" and then remain steadfast will have no fear and no grief, and that they are the people of Paradise, where they will abide forever as a reward for their deeds. The commentators explain steadfastness in closely related ways. Al-Tabari describes it as persisting in belief without mixing it with association and without disobeying God's commands and prohibitions. Al-Mawardi reports that Abu Bakr al-Siddiq understood it as remaining firm in the belief that God is their Lord, Ibn Abbas as remaining firm in the testimony that there is no god but God, and Abu al-Aliya as sincerity in religion and deed. Ibn Atiyya stresses good works, while judging Abu Bakr's view broader in its hope. Al-Razi distinguishes the fear of punishment, which departs, from awe before God's majesty, which does not. Ibn Atiyya defines fear as distress over the future and grief as distress over the past. Sa'id ibn Jubayr took grief to mean the moment of death, but the prevailing reading points to the terrors of the Day of Judgment. Several scholars note that the verse is set in the context of the unbelievers' reaction to the believers and to the conversion of 'Abd Allah ibn Salam, without changing its general meaning. Al-Qurtubi and others report that Ibn Abbas linked the verse to Abu Bakr, while its wider application to every steadfast believer is accepted.

This verse states that those who say "Our Lord is Allah" and then remain upright will have no fear regarding what lies ahead and no grief over what they leave behind, and that they are the companions of Paradise, where they will abide forever as a reward for their deeds. The commentators agree that faith and steadfastness in it are the basis of this promise, and that Paradise is a recompense for deeds rather than something owed. Abu Bakr al-Siddiq and Ibn 'Abbas explain uprightness as remaining firm in monotheism and faith, while Abu al-'Aliya understands it as sincerity in religion and action, and al-Tabari and al-Qurtubi take it in general as persistence in good works. Abu al-Su'ud and al-Baydawi link it to combining monotheism with righteous action. Sa'id ibn Jubayr holds that the grief denied is grief at the moment of death, whereas others take it as the terror of the Day of Resurrection. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi parse the word "jaza'an" as an absolute object of an implied verb. Several commentators report that the verse was revealed concerning Abu Bakr, but Ibn Kathir notes that it applies generally to every believer who stays steadfast, and the exegetes do not otherwise weigh in on this point.

God enjoins people to be good to their parents. The mother carried the child in her womb with hardship and gave birth with hardship, and the period of carrying and weaning is thirty months. Commentators link this with the verse on two years of nursing to conclude that the minimum pregnancy is six months, a view attributed to Ali and Ibn Abbas by al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi. When a person reaches full strength and forty years, he prays that God inspire him to thank Him for the blessings given to him and to his parents, to do righteous deeds that please Him, to make his offspring righteous, and he declares his repentance and submission. Al-Tabari, al-Mawardi and Ibn Kathir report that the verse was revealed about Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, whose parents and children all embraced Islam, while al-Hasan holds it is general to all believers, and some attribute it to Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas. On the age of full strength, opinions differ: thirty-three years according to Ibn Abbas and Qatada, puberty according to al-Sha'bi and Ibn Zayd, forty according to al-Hasan, and al-Zamakhshari sees forty as its end. The following verses state that God accepts the best of their deeds and overlooks their sins, placing them among the people of Paradise, as a true promise.

This verse states that those who combine repentance, kindness to their parents and righteousness towards their offspring, who are the people described in the preceding verses, will have God accept their best deeds and overlook their bad deeds, so that they will be among the people of Paradise. The commentators regard this as a true promise that will not be broken, the promise of Paradise announced to them by the messengers in this world. Readers differed over the two verbs: the majority read them in the passive with 'ahsanu' in the nominative, while Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Hafs read them with a first-person plural and 'ahsana' in the accusative, and al-Tabari held that both readings are sound in meaning. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Razi explain that 'the best' means simply 'the good', and that a permissible act is good but earns no reward, while al-Tabari takes the phrase to refer to acts that carry a reward. Most commentators link the preceding verse to Abu Bakr al-Siddiq: according to Ibn 'Abbas, al-Kalbi and Ibn Kathir, God answered his prayer so that both his parents and his children embraced Islam. Al-Hasan and Qatada hold instead that the passage is general, referring to anyone with these qualities. Ibn Kathir also cites reports attributed to Ali that name Uthman, while Aisha denied that it concerned Abd al-Rahman, son of Abu Bakr. Several commentators add that gratitude to God includes gratitude for the gift of faith, and that the duty of kindness to parents is repeated throughout the Quran.

This verse portrays the disobedient son who rejects his believing parents' call to faith in God and the resurrection. He says "Uff to you both!" and doubts he will be brought out of his grave alive, pointing out that past generations have not returned, while his parents cry out to God and urge him to believe in God's promise, which is true. He replies that their words are nothing but the fables of the ancients. The commentators largely take the verse as describing a type: al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Nasafi hold that it applies to anyone who disobeys his parents and denies the truth, while al-Hasan and Qatada see a portrait of a disbelieving, sinful servant. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and Ibn 'Atiyya also keep the collective sense of the relative pronoun, which the plural "those" that follows supports. The report that the verse concerns Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Bakr before his conversion, transmitted through Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and al-Suddi, is rejected by Aisha, and Ibn Kathir calls it weak, since conversion wipes out earlier sins. Al-Zajjaj and Ibn al-Jawzi likewise conclude it concerns an unbelieving disobedient son. The readings differ on the pronunciation of "uff" and "ata'iduanni" without changing the meaning. The passage ends by stating that each group has degrees according to deeds, and that the disbelievers exposed to the Fire will be rebuked for squandering their good things in the worldly life, for arrogance without right and for transgression. Umar ibn al-Khattab cited this verse to justify his abstention from luxury.

This verse describes a type of person whom the Qur'an portrays as disobedient and disbelieving: one of them says to his parents, "Uff to you," and denies the resurrection, asking how he could be brought out of his grave when earlier generations have never returned. The commentators explain that his parents were calling him to faith and invoking God for his guidance, but he replied that their words were merely the fables of the ancients. The verse says these people deserve God's decree, as did earlier nations of jinn and humans, and that they are losers. The exegetes differ on who is meant. Some report that the verse was revealed about Abd al-Rahman, son of Abu Bakr, before his conversion, a view held by Marwan ibn al-Hakam, Qatada and al-Suddi. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Nasafi, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Razi reject this, since Abd al-Rahman later embraced Islam and lived well, and they take the verse as a general rule for anyone who disobeys his parents and denies resurrection; al-Hasan says it describes a disbelieving rebel against his parents. As for "each has degrees according to their deeds," Ibn Zayd says the degrees of the people of Paradise rise while those of the people of Hell descend, and al-Razi applies the phrase to both believers and disbelievers. God is said to repay each person fully without injustice. The disbelievers will be rebuked on the Day of Judgment for the good things they enjoyed in the world, and for their arrogance and defiance, and will receive the punishment of humiliation. Some cite Umar ibn al-Khattab, who avoided many good things out of fear that they might diminish his good deeds.

The commentators explain that this verse closes the description of the two groups: believers who are dutiful to their parents and disbelievers who are disobedient. Each group will have ranks and degrees with God on the Day of Resurrection according to what they did in this world, good or bad, and God will repay each person in full for his deeds without wronging anyone: nothing will be added to the evildoer's punishment and nothing taken from the doer of good's reward. Most exegetes, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Nasafi and Ibn Sa'di, understand the degrees as different levels of reward, those of the people of Paradise rising while those of the people of the Fire descend, as Ibn Zayd reports. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Qurtubi and al-Alusi explain that the word 'degrees' is used here by way of dominance, since Paradise is called 'degrees' and Hell 'deeks', so the term covers both groups. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi note that the particle 'li' in 'liyuwaffiyahum' depends on a verb left implied: the reward was measured according to the deeds so that God would pay them their works in full. The readings differ between 'ya' and 'nun'; Abu 'Ubayd prefers 'nun' and Abu Hatim 'ya', the reading of most readers. Several exegetes report that the preceding verses concerned 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Bakr or someone else, but al-Tabari, Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn Kathir hold that the statement is general for any disobedient son and reject the claim that it concerns 'Abd al-Rahman, who converted and became a righteous man. Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi point out that this verse affirms reward proportionate to each deed, with no injustice to anyone.

This verse describes how, on the Day of Resurrection, those who disbelieved will be presented to the Fire and told in rebuke that they used up their good things in the life of this world and enjoyed them, so nothing of them remains for them. Today they will be recompensed with the torment of humiliation, for having been arrogant on earth without right and for having departed from obedience to God. Commentators such as al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Qurtubi, al-Nasafi and Ibn Sa'di agree that the verse addresses disbelievers, and that the reproach targets pursuing pleasures and being absorbed in luxury at the expense of the Hereafter. On the meaning of being presented to the Fire, al-Zamakhshari, Abu Hayyan and others take it as being tormented by it, or being brought close to it and shown it. Some suggest an inversion of the phrase, the Fire being presented to them, which Abu Hayyan rejects as unnecessary. On the reading of the verb, most read the declarative form, while Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir and others read the interrogative form of reproach; both are eloquent Arabic, and al-Tabari prefers the declarative. Many report the practice of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, who avoided many good foods out of fear of being among those addressed by this verse, which several present as asceticism. Ibn al-Qayyim, Ibn 'Ashur and al-Qasimi argue that the verse does not forbid believers lawful goods, and that renunciation remains the higher path. The word al-hawn is explained as humiliation. Al-Razi distinguishes arrogance, a matter of the heart, from wickedness, a matter of the limbs.

God tells His Prophet to recall the story of Hud, brother of the 'Ad in lineage but not in faith, who warned his people in the Ahqaf, a region of winding sand dunes. The commentators agree that messengers before and after him all called to the same message: worship God alone. They also agree that Hud was of the same people by descent, and that he feared for them a tremendous day of punishment. They differ on where the Ahqaf lay. Ibn 'Abbas first said it was a valley between Oman and Mahra, and in another report a mountain in Syria, a view also held by al-Dahhak. Qatada, Ibn Zayd and others place it in sand dunes overlooking the sea at al-Shihr in Yemen, while Ibn Ishaq locates it between Oman and Hadramawt. Al-Tabari declines to settle the question, noting it carries no binding religious obligation. Al-Razi and Ibn Kathir present the story as a lesson for the Meccans, whose absorption in worldly comforts blinds them to the truth. The narrative that follows is widely shared: the people of Hud demanded the punishment he promised, and he replied that the knowledge belongs to God alone. When they saw a cloud they took for rain, it was a wind carrying punishment that destroyed everything, leaving only their dwellings. Some commentators add reports of the Prophet's fear of clouds and winds. Al-Sa'di notes that Hud's clear call was rejected.

This verse reports the reply of the people of 'Ad to their prophet Hud, peace be upon him, when he called them to worship God alone and warned them of the punishment of a great day. They answered in denial: have you come to turn us away from our gods? Bring us then the punishment you threaten us with, if you are truthful. Al-Tabari, quoting Ibn Zayd, explains that 'li-ta'fikana' means to turn us away or to remove us, and al-Zamakhshari, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Razi give the same sense. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi also mention that it can mean turning them away by falsehood. The commentators agree that this answer is a rejection of the call and a mockery of it. On the location of the Ahqaf, al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir report that they are long, curved sand dunes; Ibn 'Abbas places them between 'Oman and Mahra, Qatada on the coast of Shihr in Yemen, while Mujahid and al-Dahhak locate them differently, al-Dahhak seeing a mountain in Syria. Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan note that Yemen is the region most commonly associated with 'Ad. Several commentators, including Ibn Kathir and al-Alusi, observe that the passage consoles the Prophet ﷺ in the face of his people's rejection, while al-Razi sees it as a warning to Quraysh. The exegetes do not decide between these readings; they present them side by side to clarify the meaning of the word and its context.

The commentators explain that when Hud warned his people, the 'Ad, of a dreadful day of punishment, they mocked him and demanded that the punishment be hastened. He replied that knowledge of its time belongs to God alone, that his duty is only to deliver the message entrusted to him, and that he sees his people as ignorant. The exegetes agree that the verse answers this demand for haste and that messengers were sent to warn, not to produce wonders on request. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi report that when they saw a cloud heading toward their valleys they thought it would bring rain, but it was a wind carrying punishment. Al-Mawardi, citing Ibn 'Abbas, places the Ahqaf in a valley between Oman and Mahra, while al-Dahhak puts them in a mountain in Syria, Mujahid in a land, and Ibn Zayd in long sand dunes. Ibn Kathir describes the wind lifting the litters and their riders like locusts. Al-Razi notes that earlier prophets had given the same warning. Ibn 'Ashur takes the restriction in 'knowledge is with God' as absolute, meaning that Hud had no knowledge of the hour of the punishment. Most commentators draw from the story a warning to the Quraysh to reflect on the fate of peoples who rejected their messengers.

The verse describes the moment when the people of 'Ad saw the punishment they had demanded, appearing as a cloud moving toward their valleys. Thinking it was rain after a long drought, they rejoiced, but Hud told them it was not a cloud of rain but a wind carrying painful punishment. The commentators agree that the pronoun in 'they saw it' refers either to the punishment or to the cloud that carried the wind, and that the wind destroyed everything by God's command, leaving only their dwellings, while Hud and the believers were saved. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report that rain had been withheld for a long time and that the cloud came from a valley called al-Mughith. Al-Zamakhshari suggests the pronoun may be vague and then clarified by 'a cloud', calling this the clearer reading, whereas Abu Hayyan denies that a circumstantial phrase can clarify a pronoun and prefers to link it to what they had requested. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi report that the wind lifted tents and women high into the air until they looked like locusts, and Ibn Abbas identifies the wind as the southern wind. Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi cite the hadith of 'A'isha in which the Prophet feared that a cloud might carry punishment as it had for 'Ad. Readers differ on the readings of 'is seen' and 'you see' and on 'their dwellings', which commentators note without settling. The lesson they draw is that joy can turn to loss and that demanding punishment is a sign of ignorance.

The verse describes a violent wind that God sent against the people of 'Ad. By His command it destroys everything it passes over, until nothing remains of them but their empty dwellings. The commentators explain that "everything" means what the wind was commanded to destroy, namely people, livestock and property, and not literally every existing thing. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi relate that the people, who had been deprived of rain for a long time, mistook the approaching cloud heading for their valleys for a rain cloud, when in fact it was the punishment Hud had warned of. Al-Baghawi, al-Razi and Ibn Kathir add that the wind lifted men, herds and tents between heaven and earth, that God then buried the people under sand for seven nights and eight days, and finally the wind cast them into the sea, while Hud and the believers were spared within an enclosure. Al-Tabari cites a hadith saying the wind sent against 'Ad was no larger than a ring, though the other commentators do not rule on its authenticity. On the readings, Hafs and Hamza read "yurā" in the passive with "masākinuhum" in the nominative, while the others read "tarā" with "masākinahum" in the accusative; al-Farra' and Ibn 'Atiyya find the feminine reading awkward. Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Ashur and al-Biqa'i take the destruction as a warning to the Quraysh.

This verse recalls that the people of 'Ad were given power, wealth and strong bodies greater than those granted to the Quraysh, and were given hearing, sight and hearts. None of these faculties benefited them, because they denied God's signs and used their gifts for other than their purpose, so the punishment they had mocked fell upon them. Ibn 'Abbas took the phrase 'fima in makkannakum fihi' to mean 'in what We did not give you', while al-Kisa'i and al-Nasafi read the particle 'in' as a negation, al-Mubarrad, Ibn Qutayba and al-Farra' treated it as superfluous or as equivalent to 'ma', and some took it as a conditional with an omitted answer, a reading Ibn 'Atiyya called overly strained. The commentators agree that the verse warns the Meccans and reminds them of earlier nations. Al-Razi, al-Biqa'i and Ibn 'Ashur explain why hearing is singular while sight and hearts are plural. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and others report that God destroyed the peoples around Mecca, such as 'Ad, Thamud, the people of Lot and Madyan, and that the gods they had taken as means of drawing near to God failed them. Al-Zamakhshari reads 'idh' as causal, so that the lack of benefit is tied to their denial. All conclude that neither strength, wealth nor faculties protect one who denies God's signs and persists in disbelief.

The commentators explain that God warns the Quraysh by reminding them of the nearby peoples He destroyed, such as ʿAd, Thamud, the people of Lot, Saba and Madyan. He set out the signs in many forms so that they might turn back from disbelief, yet they did not turn back. The next verse adds that the idols they took as intercessors to draw near to God did not help them when punishment came, but abandoned them, and that this was the outcome of their lies and fabrications. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Juzayy agree that the word 'towns' refers to their inhabitants, and that the address is to the Quraysh as a warning. Al-Baghawi and others note that the proofs given were sufficient had they accepted them. Ibn ʿAshur holds that the variation of signs covers argument, threat, warning and reminder of blessings. On the reading of 'ifkuhum', al-Tabari, Ibn ʿAtiyya and Abu Hayyan report that the majority read it with a kasra on the alif and a sukun on the fa, while Ibn ʿAbbas and others read it with fathas, giving it the sense of turning away. al-Tabari upholds the reading of the major cities. As for the grammatical role of 'qurbanan', al-Zamakhshari makes it a circumstantial accusative and rejects that it be a second object, whereas Ibn ʿAtiyya and Abu Hayyan allow it without, in their view, corrupting the meaning.

This verse recalls that God destroyed the towns around Mecca, such as 'Ad, Thamud, Sodom and Ma'rib, after showing them signs and proofs so that they might turn back from disbelief. It then asks, in rebuke, why the gods they had taken besides God as means of drawing near to Him did not help them. The implied answer is that these gods abandoned them and were absent when they were needed, and that this was the result of their lies and fabrications. The commentators agree that the aim is to warn the Meccan polytheists and to mock the idols that could not intervene when punishment came. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi identify the towns as those of 'Ad, Thamud, the people of Lot and Midian, while Ibn Juzayy and Abu Hayyan see them as examples addressed to Quraysh through Ma'rib, Hijr, Thamud and Sodom. On the word 'qurbanan', al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi explain it as that by which one draws near to God, and treat it as a circumstantial phrase; Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan allow it to be the second object of the verb, which al-Zamakhshari rejects because it spoils the meaning. For the reading of 'ifkuhum', the majority reads it with a kasra and a sukun, whereas Ibn 'Abbas and others read 'afakahum' meaning that it turned them from the truth; al-Tabari upholds the reading of the major cities. Al-Razi and al-Alusi note the ironic tone of the passage and the impossibility of any help, along with the different readings of 'ma kanu yaftarun', which can be a verbal clause or a relative clause.

This verse recounts that a small group of jinn, fewer than ten, were turned toward the Prophet ﷺ while he recited the Quran. When they were present they told one another to be silent and listen, and when the recitation ended they returned to their people as warners. The commentators agree that the passage rebukes the Quraysh, who did not believe although the jinn did. They differ on the circumstances. Ibn 'Abbas and Sa'id ibn Jubayr report that the jinn, who had been struck by shooting stars guarding the sky, sought the cause and found the Prophet praying the dawn prayer at Nakhla without his noticing them. Others, including Ibn Mas'ud, report that the Prophet was commanded to recite to the jinn, that Ibn Mas'ud followed him and was drawn a line, that he heard a loud commotion, and that the Prophet afterward explained he had judged a dispute among them over a slain man. On their number, Ibn 'Abbas said seven from Nisibis, Zirr ibn Hubaysh said nine including Zawba'a, and 'Ikrima said twelve thousand. On their reward, Abu Hanifa held that they have no reward beyond being saved from the Fire, while Malik, al-Shafi'i and Ibn Abi Layla held that they are rewarded for good deeds as they are punished for evil. The jinn declare that the Book confirms what came before it and guides to truth and the straight path, and they urge their people to answer God's caller and believe, for whoever does not answer is in clear error.

This verse reports what a group of jinn said to their people after hearing the Prophet ﷺ recite. They describe a Book revealed after Moses that confirms the earlier scriptures and guides to the truth and to a straight path. The commentators agree that this Book is the Quran and that the jinn delivered a warning to their people. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi report that these jinn came from Nisibis, Nineveh or the Mosul region, and the reports on their number differ: seven or nine according to Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and Zirr ibn Hubaysh, and twelve thousand according to Ikrima. Many hold that the Prophet did not notice them at first, whereas al-Hasan al-Basri says he learned of them only through revelation. On the mention of Moses without Jesus, Ibn Abbas explains that the jinn had not heard of Jesus, while al-Zamakhshari, al-Biqa'i and Ibn Kathir see it as recognition that the Torah is the foundation of the law. On the reward of believing jinn, Abu Hanifa holds that they gain only deliverance from the Fire, while Malik, al-Shafi'i and Ibn Abi Layla hold that they are treated like humans, rewarded for good and punished for evil; Ibn Kathir cites Surat al-Rahman to argue they enter Paradise. Ibn Kathir and al-Bayhaqi relate that delegations of jinn came to the Prophet repeatedly afterwards, the most accepted view placing the first encounter about three years before the Hijra.

This passage reports the words of the jinn who, after listening to the Qur'an and returning to their people as warners, told them: answer the summoner of God, that is the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, believe in him and obey what he brings; God will forgive you some of your sins and protect you from a painful punishment. The commentators agree on this plain meaning: a call to faith and obedience, with the promise of forgiveness and deliverance from the Fire. Many, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Nasafi, al-Shawkani, Ibn Juzayy and Abu Hayyan, note that the word "min" in "some of your sins" makes the forgiveness partial, so that wrongs done to people are forgiven only when restitution is made to their owners. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya also read it as partitive, since faith does not wipe out every sin; others take it as superfluous or as indicating a starting point. On the reward of believing jinn, opinions differ. Abu Hanifa, as reported by al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi, held that they gain only deliverance from the Fire; Malik, al-Shafi'i and Ibn Abi Layla held that they are rewarded for good deeds as humans are, and al-Dahhak reported that they enter Paradise. Ibn Kathir cites the verse in Surat al-Rahman in support of the entry of believing jinn into Paradise. As for the phrase "whoever does not answer God's summoner cannot escape Him on earth", it warns that flight offers no escape from God, that there are no protectors besides Him, and that those who refuse are in clear error. Several commentators report that these jinn came from Nisibis or Nineveh, that the event took place at Batn Nakhla during the dawn prayer, and they differ on whether Ibn Mas'ud was present, a point that does not directly affect the meaning of the verse.

The verse says that whoever does not answer God's call, conveyed by His Messenger ﷺ, cannot escape God on earth, and has no protectors apart from Him; such people are in clear error. The commentators connect this passage to the account of the jinn who heard the Qur'an and returned to their people as warners. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi explain that not answering means not believing or obeying, and that no one can flee divine power. Ibn 'Ashur and others note that the words may be spoken by the jinn or by God Himself, and Ibn Kathir draws no legal conclusion from it. The main debate concerns the reward of believing jinn: Abu Hanifa holds that they receive only deliverance from the Fire, while al-Razi, al-Qurtubi, Malik and Ibn Abi Layla argue that they face the same reward and punishment as humans. Ibn Kathir leans toward the believing jinn entering Paradise, without stating it as certain. On the particle 'min' in 'min dhunubikum', al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Juzayy take it as partitive, excluding wrongs done to people, while al-Razi reads it as marking a starting point. These disputes do not change the general meaning of the verse, on which all agree."}

In this verse, God reminds those who deny resurrection that they have not considered that the One who created the heavens and the earth without being wearied by it is able to bring the dead back to life. The commentators explain that the verb ya'ya means to be weary or unable, that the question is rhetorical and reproachful, and that the closing affirmation 'bala' confirms God's power over everything. They agree that the verse is an argument for resurrection moving from the greater to the lesser: whoever can create the heavens and the earth can recreate a human being. Grammarians differ on the particle ba in 'bi-qadir'. Abu 'Ubayda and al-Akhfash consider it an emphatic particle with no meaning of its own. Al-Kisa'i, al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj explain it by the negation that precedes 'inna', so that the sense is 'Is God not able?'. Al-Tabari judges this last view the most sound. Ibn Kathir reports that God said to the heavens and the earth 'Be', and they obeyed without resistance. Several commentators note that the reading yaqdir, transmitted from Ya'qub, avoids this grammatical issue. The exegetes conclude by stressing that this power extends to everything, and that denying resurrection amounts to denying the universality of God's power.

The verse depicts the Day of Resurrection when the disbelievers are presented before the Fire. They are asked, as a rebuke, whether this is not the truth; they confess, "Yes, by our Lord!" and are told, "Taste the punishment for what you used to deny." The commentators agree that this is a rebuke and a mockery of those who scoffed at God's promise and threat, and that their confession comes too late to benefit them. Al-Hasan al-Basri adds that they will be punished while content with it, acknowledging God's justice. As for the command that the Prophet be patient as the messengers of resolve were patient, opinions differ on who they are. Ibn Zayd, al-Tabari and Ibn al-Anbari hold that they are all the messengers, with "min" meaning "namely" rather than "some of"; Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada and Mujahid name Noah, Abraham, Moses, Jesus and Muhammad; Muqatil counts six, al-Hasan al-Basri four, and al-Hasan ibn al-Fadl the eighteen prophets of the chapter of the Cattle. All agree that the sense is patience under harm and striving, and that the Prophet must not hasten the punishment for his people. The disbelievers, the commentators note, will feel they stayed in the world only an hour of a day. On the word "balagh", some take it as the Qur'an or the delivery of the message, others as the length of earthly life. The verse ends with a warning to the defiantly wicked, which several scholars regard as a source of hope for believers.

This verse tells the Prophet ﷺ to be patient in the face of his people's rejection, as the steadfast messengers were patient, and not to seek the punishment of the disbelievers, which will certainly come. The commentators explain that on the day they see it, the disbelievers will feel that they lived in this world for no more than an hour of a day. The verse ends by stating that the Qur'an is a message delivered, and that only the defiant who depart from obedience to God are destroyed.

The commentators agree that the patience commanded means steadfastness in conveying the message and bearing harm. The identity of the messengers of firm resolve, however, is disputed. Ibn Abbas, Qatada, Ata al-Khurasani and Ibn Kathir name Noah, Abraham, Moses, Jesus and Muhammad ﷺ. Al-Kalbi, Muqatil and al-Hasan ibn al-Fadl give longer lists, some reaching eighteen prophets. Ibn Zayd and Ibn al-Anbari hold that "min" is explanatory rather than partitive, so that all messengers are meant.

On the word "balagh", al-Tabari, Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn Kathir offer two readings: it refers either to the Qur'an and its message, or to the short duration of life just mentioned. Several commentators, including Qatada, stress the hopeful note of the closing phrase: only the one who deserves it is destroyed before God.
